expected.title: Different Roles in Society
expected.content:
Bayani leads you to a gathering in the community.

“Explorer, you learned how a datu could help lead a community,” Bayani says. “But did everyone have the same role?”

You notice that people have different responsibilities. Some belong to families with greater influence. Others have more freedom to make their own choices, while some must serve or work for others because of their social position.

“Does everyone have the same rights?” you ask.

“Not always,” Bayani answers. “In some early Filipino societies, a person's place in society affected their rights and duties.”

Bayani shows you two sets of historical terms.

“In some Visayan communities, people used terms such as tumao, timawa, and oripun. In some Tagalog communities, terms included maginoo, maharlika, and alipin.”

“Are those groups exactly the same?” you ask.

“No,” Bayani replies. “Different communities had different social systems. We should not assume that their groups had exactly the same roles or rights.”

Bayani turns to you.

“Your next investigation is to discover how social position could affect people's lives. Look carefully, Explorer. Not everyone experienced community life in the same way!”
expected.imageAlt: Storybook illustration of people with different activities and responsibilities in an early Philippine coastal community.
expected.imageCaption: People in early Philippine societies had different roles, rights, and responsibilities. These varied across communities.
expected.exploreIntroduction: Lira has found four clues about social groups in early Philippine communities. Explore each clue to discover how people's positions could affect their rights and responsibilities.

exploreItems.title: Clue 1: Influential Families
exploreItems.hint: Did some families have greater influence than others?
exploreItems.discovery: In some early Philippine societies, certain families held greater influence and authority. In some Tagalog communities, the term maginoo referred to a high-status group. In some Visayan communities, tumao was associated with high-ranking families.

exploreItems.title: Clue 2: Free Community Members
exploreItems.hint: Did everyone outside the leading families have the same duties?
exploreItems.discovery: Some community members had personal freedom but also responsibilities to their leaders or communities. Historical accounts use the term maharlika for a group in some Tagalog societies and timawa for a group in some Visayan societies. Their roles were not exactly the same.

exploreItems.title: Clue 3: Different Obligations
exploreItems.hint: Could a person's social position limit their choices?
exploreItems.discovery: In some early Philippine societies, certain people had obligations to serve others. Historical accounts use terms such as alipin in Tagalog communities and oripun in Visayan communities. Their situations varied, and these terms did not always describe the same conditions.

exploreItems.hint: Were social groups identical in every early Philippine community?
exploreItems.title: Clue 4: Comparing Communities
exploreItems.discovery: Early Philippine communities did not all have the same social system. The names, rights, and duties of social groups could differ across places and periods. Historians study these differences to better understand people's lives.

expected.decisionSituation:
Lira shows you two descriptions from early Philippine societies. One describes a maharlika in a Tagalog community. The other describes a timawa in a Visayan community. Both had responsibilities, but their roles were not necessarily the same.
“Explorer,” Lira asks, “how should we compare these two groups?”
expected.decisionQuestion: What is the best way to understand these two historical groups?
decisionChoices: Treat the two groups as identical because both had responsibilities.
Compare their rights and duties while remembering that their communities had different customs.
Assume that the group with more duties always had less freedom.
Use the customs of one community to explain every other community.
expected.decisionCorrectAnswer: Compare their rights and duties while remembering that their communities had different customs.
expected.decisionExplanation: Historical groups from different communities should not automatically be treated as identical. Their rights, responsibilities, and relationships could differ. Comparing these details helps us understand early Philippine societies more accurately.
expected.discoveryTitle: Discovery Unlocked: Different Roles in Society
expected.discoveryText: You discovered that people in early Philippine societies did not always have the same rights and responsibilities. Some belonged to influential families, others had greater personal freedom, and some had obligations to serve others. Social groups differed across communities, so historians compare their roles carefully.
expected.keyTermDefinition: A person's position in society. In some early Philippine communities, social status could affect a person's rights, duties, and opportunities.
expected.historicalInsight: Early Philippine societies had different social groups. In some communities, a person's social position affected their rights, responsibilities, and relationships with others. Historical accounts describe groups such as maginoo, maharlika, and alipin in Tagalog societies, and tumao, timawa, and oripun in some Visayan societies. These groups were not identical across regions, and their roles could change over time.

fields.title: Compare Social Position, Duties and Freedom
fields.content:
Chapter 1 showed different kinds of work. Social status means a person's position in society. It is more than a job: it can affect recognized rights, duties and freedom. The same task does not mean two people have the same choices.

Use a specific example rather than one pyramid for every island. Juan de Plasencia, a Spanish missionary writing in 1589, described Tagalog communities using terms including maharlika and different forms of alipin. His account is one outside view, written after Spanish arrival, not the voice of every community.

In that account, maharlika were free people with duties to a datu. Aliping namamahay could live in their own homes and have property while owing service. Aliping sa gigilid served within another household, with greater restrictions; the account says people in this category could be sold. These were unequal conditions, not simply voluntary jobs.

Other sources use terms such as timawa, and social arrangements varied. Do not automatically match every Tagalog label with a Visayan label. Compare the place, source, duties and freedoms before deciding whether two groups were alike.
fields.imageAlt: One 1589 Tagalog account: maharlika were free people with service duties; aliping namamahay could have their own homes and property while owing service; aliping sa gigilid served in another household under greater restrictions and could be sold in the account. This is not a universal social pyramid.
fields.imageCaption: Teaching comparison, not a photograph or a universal social pyramid. A historical position is not a measure of human worth.

expected.title: Responsibilities and Fairness
expected.content:
Bayani takes you to a gathering in an early Filipino community.

“Explorer, we already learned that people could have different social positions,” Bayani says. “But how did those differences affect their lives?”

You notice two people preparing for a community gathering.

One person can choose when to leave and visit relatives. Another person must first complete work owed to someone else.

“Why can't they both make the same choice?” you ask.

“In some early Philippine societies, people's rights and duties depended partly on their social position and relationships,” Bayani explains.

You watch as the second person finishes the required work before joining the gathering.

“That doesn't seem like the same amount of freedom,” you say.

“You noticed something important,” Bayani replies. “People did not always have equal choices. To understand history, we should learn about those differences instead of assuming everyone lived the same way.”

Bayani turns to you.

“Your mission is to investigate how rights and responsibilities could affect people's choices. What can these differences teach us about life in the past?”

fields.title: Your Turn: Compare Two People
fields.content:
Now apply the comparison to two made-up people. Their names and circumstances are teaching examples, not biographies of actual historical individuals.

Person A owes an agreed task at a gathering, but can choose to visit relatives after finishing. Person B must continue required service in another household and cannot decide freely to leave. Both are working, yet the information describes different limits on choice. We cannot assign their exact historical titles from these brief descriptions alone.

Work through the evidence. Step 1. Identify what each person must do. Step 2. Identify which choices each can make. Step 3. Explain the difference without judging the worth of either person. A duty is something someone is expected or required to do. Freedom of choice concerns what they can decide for themselves.

Not every duty was freely accepted, and describing a custom does not make an unequal arrangement fair. Do not turn historical social labels into names for classmates or a game of owning people. Use the supplied cases to understand experiences and their limits.

expected.title: Understanding Early Filipino Society
expected.content:
Bayani welcomes you to the final investigation of your mission.

“Explorer, you've discovered many things about early Filipino societies. Now it's time to connect the clues!”

Bayani shows you a drawing of a community gathering.

A datu is speaking with several families. An elder is sharing advice about a community custom. Relatives are helping one another prepare for the gathering.

You also notice that people have different duties. Some can choose how to spend their time, while others have work they are expected to complete.

“There's so much happening in one community!” you say.

“That's right,” Bayani replies. “Leaders, families, customs, and social relationships all helped shape people's lives.”

Bayani shows you another drawing from a different early Philippine community.

“Look carefully. Some practices and social groups are different here.”

“So early Filipino communities weren't all exactly alike?” you ask.

“Exactly! Their ways of life could differ depending on their location, traditions, and relationships.”

Bayani smiles.

“Your final challenge is to study the clues and explain what they reveal about early Filipino society. Ready, Explorer?”
expected.exploreIntroduction: Bayani has prepared four final clues. Connect what you learned about leadership, social groups, family ties, and customs to understand how early Filipino communities worked.

exploreItems.discovery: A datu could help guide community affairs and address disagreements. Leadership practices and authority varied among early Philippine communities.
exploreItems.title: Final Clue 1: Leadership
exploreItems.hint: How could a datu help guide a community?

exploreItems.discovery: In some early Philippine societies, people's social positions and relationships affected their rights, duties, and freedom. These arrangements were not identical across communities.
exploreItems.hint: Did everyone have the same rights and responsibilities?
exploreItems.title: Final Clue 2: Social Relationships

exploreItems.discovery: Family ties could connect relatives across households. Older family members could share stories and traditions, while relatives could help one another.
exploreItems.title: Final Clue 3: Family Connections
exploreItems.hint: How could relatives support one another?
How could customs guide people's actions?
exploreItems.discovery: Community customs could guide behavior, agreements, and relationships. People could learn these practices from older generations, and customs differed among communities.
exploreItems.title: Final Clue 4: Community Customs

expected.decisionSituation:
Bayani shows you two descriptions of early Philippine communities.
In one community, a datu helps settle disagreements, and families follow local customs. Some people have different rights and duties because of their social positions.
In another community, people also have leaders, family relationships, and traditions, but their social groups and customs are not exactly the same.
Bayani asks, “Explorer, what conclusion can you make from these clues?”
expected.decisionQuestion: What is the most accurate conclusion about early Philippine societies?
decisionChoices: Every early Philippine community followed exactly the same customs and social system.
Only leaders and influential families played a role in community life.
Early Philippine communities had leaders, family ties, and customs, but their social arrangements could differ.
Family relationships and community customs had no effect on people's lives.
expected.decisionCorrectAnswer: Early Philippine communities had leaders, family ties, and customs, but their social arrangements could differ.
expected.decisionExplanation: Many early Philippine communities had recognized leaders, family relationships, customs, and social responsibilities. However, these features were not identical everywhere. Comparing communities helps us understand both their similarities and differences.
expected.discoveryTitle: Final Discovery Unlocked: Understanding Early Filipino Society
expected.discoveryText: Mission investigation complete! You discovered how leaders, social groups, family connections, and customs could shape life in early Philippine communities. You also learned that people's rights, duties, and traditions were not the same everywhere. Understanding these differences helps us see a fuller picture of Philippine history.
expected.keyTermDefinition: A group of people who live together or are connected through shared relationships, customs, and ways of organizing community life.
expected.historicalInsight: Early Philippine communities had varied forms of leadership, family relationships, customs, and social organization. In many communities, a datu was a recognized leader, while family ties and customary practices helped shape relationships. Some societies also had social groups with different rights and obligations. These arrangements differed across regions and periods, so historians avoid treating all early Philippine communities as identical.

fields.title: Field Journal: Connect Community Experiences
fields.content:
Connect the mission discoveries. A datu could help guide community affairs. Family ties could connect relatives across households. Customs could be passed through stories, advice and everyday practice. Social positions could affect rights and duties, so people did not experience community life in one identical way.

Use the comparison method in your journal: name the source and setting, describe a responsibility, identify a choice or restriction, then state what remains uncertain. The title of a leader alone does not explain every action, and seeing people cooperate does not prove that everyone had equal freedom.

Our Tagalog source example is not a description of all Philippine communities. The fictional cases help you practise comparing choices; they do not give an exact title to every person. Save useful opened clues if you want to revisit the evidence. Next, the beliefs-and-traditions mission asks how people understood their world and passed on knowledge, while keeping differences among communities visible.
